newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-China to blow away Hong Kong's democratic winds.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-China to blow away Hong Kong's democratic winds.

text.p: China has gagged its tiny band of dissidents in the run-up to Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule and is determined to stop the territory's democratic winds from blowing its way.
"The mainland dissident movement pretty much has been smashed," Robin Munro of Human Rights Watch said in a telephone interview from Hong Kong.
"There's hardly anything left of it," Munro said. "It is pretty dismal ... Worse than I can remember for the last 20 years."
International human rights groups and Western governments have accused Beijing of effectively silencing all public dissent by the end of 1996 through jailings, intimidation or exile.

China considers dissidents common criminals and rejects criticism of its human rights record as interference in its internal affairs, arguing that the right to the bare necessities of life is more important than political rights.

Beijing's gag on dissidents is part of its eagerness to ensure nothing goes wrong as Britain prepares to hand back Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of colonial rule. HONG KONG'S DEMOCRATIC WINDS UNLIKELY TO FAN CHINA
But Hong Kong's democratic winds -- a free press and multi-party politics -- are unlikely to blow in China's direction.

"Hong Kong is Hong Kong. The mainland is the mainland," Li Youwei, Communist Party boss in the southern city of Shenzhen, told reporters recently when asked if the return of Hong Kong might cause instability in China.
"The bounds of 'one country, two systems' must never be broken," Li added.
Under the "one country, two systems" formula, communist China promises that Hong Kong can keep its capitalist lifestyle and enjoy a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the handover.
But confidence in the pledge was dented in June 1989 when Chinese soldiers backed by tanks crushed student-led demonstrations for democracy in Beijing's Tiananmen Square, killing hundreds.

About 55,000 people poured into a Hong Kong park for a candlelit vigil on the eighth anniversary of the crackdown on June 4 this year to mourn victims, ignoring a plea from the territory's future leader Tung Chee-hwa to forget Tiananmen Square in the interests of a "smooth transition".

Tung had urged Hong Kong residents to look instead to the future and set aside the "baggage of June 4". But images of the crackdown are still vivid in the memories of many of the colony's 6.4 million residents. CRACKDOWN SEEN IF HONG KONG BECOMES BASE FOR REBELS
Hong Kong Chief Secretary Anson Chan has warned that China would crack down on the territory if it became a base for subversion after Beijing resumes control.
For many Chinese dissidents, Hong Kong has been a haven where they could seek refuge and a political paradise where they can publish what they could not at home.
"Political ideas and views that could not be expressed or published in the mainland can be expressed or published in Hong Kong," Munro said.
Britain has secretly granted political asylum to five Chinese dissidents recently based in Hong Kong, said the Independent on Sunday newspaper.
One was a student leader of the 1989 pro-democracy movement.
"They have been granted full political asylum in Britain with rights to social benefis, the immediate right to work and the right to a British passport after four years."

The paper quoted one of the unidentified dissidents as saying the move was arranged in cooperation with the Hong Kong government, British officials and human rights groups. The dissident was now living in Britain under a new name, it said.

Fearful of China's political clout after it takes back Hong Kong, scores of mainland dissidents have fled abroad in recent months, Frank Lu, a spokesman of the Information Centre of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in China, told Reuters in Hong Kong.

Six left for Sweden last week, among them Shao Jiang, one of the student activists who took part in the pro-democracy movement in Beijing in 1989. The British-led administration, Lu said, which had helped dozens of dissidents find sanctuary in the run up to the handover, was now too preoccupied with their own departure.

Many people, including dissident Ren Wanding, who was jailed for seven years for his role in the 1989 demonstrations, long for the freedoms Hong Kong residents enjoy. "We envy Hong Kong for its degree of freedom," Ren told Reuters by telephone.
But much of that could change after the handover.
"With the return of Hong Kong to China ... that will no longer exist," he said. "There will be a sense of loss among the few dissidents left ... and dissidents in jail."
"The government has always been extremely paranoid ... about the role dissidents can play in serving as ... a fuse to ignite a much broader popular discontent in society," Munro said.

"They are obsessed with what they see as this danger or threat to their power," he added. "It would be naive for the international community to anticipate any fundamental softening of Beijing's intense hostility to democratic tendencies or the dissident movement."
